# Part 7: Organizational Adoption

## 7.1 The adoption problem

The technology works. That fact is now cheap and decides almost nothing. In an enterprise artificial intelligence portfolio, the systems that fail overwhelmingly do so after working in a controlled setting, on causes no model evaluation detects: nobody was given access, those given access were never told what the system could not do, reviewers were never given time, the champions left, the workflow was never changed so the system sat beside the work rather than inside it, and the first confident wrong answer landed on the desk of the one partner whose opinion the department follows.

**Adoption is an architectural property, not a downstream campaign**, designed at the same moment as the retrieval strategy and failing for reasons as structural as any latency budget.

There are exactly **three adoption failures**, presenting differently and diagnosed differently.

| Failure | Presentation | Correct diagnosis | Wrong fix commonly applied | Correct fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nobody uses it** | Provisioned population far exceeds active population. Usage concentrated in the build team and their friends. Flat or declining first-touch curve | Access friction, awareness gap, no trigger inside the workflow, or the use case does not match a real task anyone is measured on | More training. Training does not create a reason to start | Put the entry point inside the tool where the work already happens, remove the provisioning step, and attach the system to a task the person is already accountable for |
| **People use it and stop** | Strong first-touch, collapse between week two and week six. Cohort curves that fall and never flatten | The system failed on the cases the user actually cared about, or the review burden exceeded the drafting saving, or an early wrong answer cost them credibility | A relaunch, a new name, an executive email. Reintroduction to an audience that already formed a judgment is the least effective intervention available | Instrument abandonment, interview the abandoned, fix the segment that failed, and return to those users individually with the specific fix named |
| **People use it wrongly** | High and rising usage, quality incidents, outputs entering the record without review, prompts containing data the classification forbids, results cited as authority | The accountability position was never taught, the limits were never stated, and the control was advisory rather than enforced | A policy reminder. Policy does not constrain behavior it cannot detect | Enforce at the system boundary rather than by instruction, teach failure recognition rather than capability, and make the review step a gate rather than a suggestion |

**Decision rule: diagnose which of the three it is before proposing any intervention, because every intervention that helps one worsens at least one other.**

The third failure is the dangerous one for a regulated enterprise and the one the usual metrics reward: a dashboard reporting seats, sessions and tokens rises fastest when it is running. Wrong use is enthusiastic use.

### The failure beneath the three

All three are downstream of one design error: **building the system beside the workflow rather than inside it**. A system that requires the user to leave the matter management platform, the claims desktop, the ticketing queue or the document management system imposes a switching cost on every interaction, forever. It is paid by the least motivated user first, the population whose adoption determines whether the program has enterprise or departmental value.

## 7.2 Pilots and the first use case

Four activities are routinely called by each other's names. The substitution is not vocabulary sloppiness; it is how an organization spends eighteen months proving what it already knew.

| Activity | Entry criteria | Exit criteria | Duration | Population | What it proves | What it cannot prove |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Proof of concept** | A specific technical uncertainty stated as a question, plus representative data | The uncertainty resolved either way, with a written answer | 2 to 6 weeks | Build team only, no real users | That a technical approach can produce an acceptable output on representative inputs | Value, adoption, cost at volume, operational viability, control adequacy, anything about people |
| **Pilot** | Working system, evaluation harness, baseline measured, control layer sufficient for real data, named business owner, defined success threshold, kill criterion | Threshold met or missed on the pre-registered metric, with a scale decision taken | 6 to 12 weeks | Bounded real population doing real work, 20 to 200 users | Value in a real workflow, adoption behavior, real error profile, reviewer load, unit economics at small scale | Scale economics, cross-segment generalization, edge-case coverage, second-order effects, what happens when the enthusiasts are no longer the users |
| **Production rollout** | Passed readiness gate, control layer complete, named operational owner who is not the architect, support model, rollback path | Steady-state operation with quality, cost and adoption inside agreed bands | Continuous | Full eligible population, staged | That the organization can run it | Nothing further. It is the thing itself |
| **Science project** | Curiosity and available budget | None defined | Indefinite | Its own team | That the technology is interesting | Anything the enterprise needed to know |

The fourth row is not a joke. A science project is identifiable by one property: **no stated decision depends on its outcome.** Science projects are not always wrong, and a research function may hold two or three legitimately, but one consuming a delivery budget under a pilot's name is a governance failure and should be named as one.

**Decision rule: if you cannot state the decision that the activity's result will change, it is a science project regardless of what the steering deck calls it.**

### Choosing the first use case

The entry point of an adoption program is an organizational question before a technical one; which surface the solution uses is the delivery-route decision of 2.8.

Five criteria select it: **high enough value to be noticed, low enough complexity to succeed, a measurable baseline so improvement can be demonstrated, a willing owner and tolerable consequences if it fails.** This is the value against complexity grid of 2.4 applied to adoption sequencing rather than a single design.

### The pilot design method

Structure the first engagement to produce a decision rather than a demonstration. Eight elements deliver that, all fixed in writing before the first user is onboarded; a pilot missing any one produces only an impression.

1. **The hypothesis**, stated so it can be false. Not "artificial intelligence will improve contract review" but "first-pass review of nondisclosure agreements will complete in under twelve minutes against a measured baseline of thirty-one, with issue-detection recall at or above the current human first-pass rate on the labeled set."
2. **The population**, named and bounded, with the selection basis stated. Volunteers measure enthusiasm; a representative draw measures the enterprise. Disclose which you chose: a volunteer pilot that succeeds says almost nothing about the general population and is the most common way pilots mislead.
3. **The control**, what the result is compared against. Three legitimate options: a pre-measured baseline on the same population, a matched holdout group running the current process or a stepped introduction across teams. Comparison against unmeasured memory is not a control, and it is what most pilots use.
4. **The duration**, fixed in advance, long enough to pass the novelty window. Six weeks is the practical floor because weeks one and two measure curiosity.
5. **The instrumentation**, decided before launch, covering usage, outcome quality, reviewer time, escalation rate, correction rate and cost per completed task. Instrumentation added later cannot describe the period before it existed, the period the decision turns on.
6. **The success threshold**, a number, pre-registered. Post-hoc thresholds are advocacy. If the sponsor will not commit in advance, that refusal is itself the finding, to be escalated rather than accommodated.
7. **The kill criterion**, a number or condition that ends the pilot early. It is the element most often omitted and the one that gives the pilot its integrity; a pilot that cannot fail is a demonstration.
8. **The decision forum and date**, named in advance, with the person who will decide identified by role. Without this the pilot ends by evaporation.

### Pilot purgatory and how to design out of it

**Pilot purgatory** is a growing inventory of pilots, none killed and none scaled. It is not caused by indecision but by four structural properties, each removable at design time.

| Cause | Mechanism | Design-time removal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **No pre-registered threshold** | Every result is arguable, so no result forces a decision | Fix the number before launch and record it where the sponsor cannot revise it |
| **No kill criterion** | Stopping requires someone to volunteer to have been wrong | Write the kill condition into the charter so stopping is compliance rather than defeat |
| **Scale funding not sequenced with the pilot** | The pilot succeeds into a budget cycle that closed four months ago | Secure conditional scale funding at pilot approval, released on the threshold |
| **The pilot built on scaffolding** | Manual data loads, a hand-curated corpus, the architect answering questions in a chat channel. None of it survives multiplication | Build the pilot on the production data path and the production control layer, accepting a slower start |

**Decision rule: fund the pilot and the conditional scale decision in the same approval, or the pilot dies of a budget calendar rather than of evidence.**

### The successful pilot that cannot scale

The distinctive enterprise pattern, and the most expensive because it consumes credibility as well as money: the pilot met its threshold honestly, then scaling failed. **Four causes**, separable at design time.

| Cause | What happened | The detection question to ask during pilot design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Population non-representativeness** | The pilot ran on volunteers, on the strongest team or in the cleanest jurisdiction. The general population has different tasks, lower tolerance and worse data | Who is in this pilot, who is not and what do the excluded do differently? |
| **Scaffolded operations** | Data was hand-prepared, exceptions were handled by the architect, the corpus was curated once. Multiply by forty and the human scaffolding is the binding constraint | If this ran for four thousand users on Monday, what task would a person be doing that they are doing now? |
| **Economics inverted by volume** | Unit cost fell but reviewer time did not, so total cost grew linearly with adoption while savings did not. Or cache economics that held at low concurrency stopped holding | What is fully loaded cost per completed task at one times, ten times and one hundred times pilot volume? |
| **Control layer sized for a pilot** | Permissions were coarse because everyone in the pilot could see everything. At scale the corpus spans entitlements, jurisdictions, matters and clients, and the retrieval layer has no way to express that | Does the pilot's authorization model survive contact with the full corpus, or did the small population hide the problem? |

The third and fourth kill programs, because a pilot hides them by construction: a twelve-person pilot inside one practice group has no entitlement problem, so no entitlement design gets built, so the rollout hits a permissions wall six weeks in and stops.

### Sequencing expansion

Choose the **second use case to reuse the first one's infrastructure** rather than to impress, and the **third to prove generality**. The user-level form of the same discipline appears in 7.3: expand by adjacent workflow, not by adjacent department.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** At what point does the second use case reusing the first one's infrastructure turn a project into a platform, and whose budget carries it?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Picking the first use case on value against complexity | Scoring and sequencing a funded backlog against capacity | Use case portfolio, owned by the investment committee |
| Choosing the second use case for reuse | Platform funding, a service catalog entry and chargeback to consuming functions | Funding model, owned by the platform owner |
| Expecting adoption after a pilot | Training, communication and measurement of adoption as distinct from availability | Adoption plan, owned by the change lead |
| Treating retirement as one line in the rollout plan | Data disposition, dependency check and exit rights across the delivery routes | **The decommissioning plan specified in 10.6, owned by the service owner.** Data disposition and dependency unwinding are two of its six workstreams; exit rights across the routes are scope this section adds to the same plan rather than a second plan |

**What this costs the organization.** Pilots die at the handover from project funding to run funding rather than at technical failure; the gap is organizational. The forgotten cost is lock-in: prompts, evaluation sets and retrieval indexes that are not portable make the next commercial negotiation one-sided.

**The executive translation.** The second use case is where this becomes a platform, which needs its own budget line and a service owner rather than another project.

## 7.3 Measuring adoption

### The adoption funnel

Six stages, each with one metric and one distinct failure. Report all six or you are reporting a number that cannot be acted on.

```
  STAGE          METRIC                     FAILURE AT THIS STAGE
  -----          ------                     ---------------------
  AWARE       %  of eligible who know       communication gap
    |            it exists and what for
    v
  PROVISIONED %  with working access        access friction, licensing,
    |            (login + entitlement)      approval queue
    v
  ACTIVATED   %  who completed one real     no trigger in the workflow;
    |            task, not a demo           first task chosen badly
    v
  HABITUAL    %  active in 4 of last 6      value not felt; review
    |            weeks on real work         burden exceeds saving
    v
  DEPENDENT   %  who would escalate if      never reached: system is
    |            it were unavailable        peripheral to real work
    v
  ADVOCATE    %  who onboarded another      no social proof; the
                 user or contributed a      program relies on push
                 correction / template      forever
```

Two rules. **The ratio between adjacent stages diagnoses; the absolute numbers do not**: eighty percent provisioned and nine percent activated is a workflow-entry problem no amount of awareness work will move. **Dependency is the only stage that predicts survival of a budget cycle**: a system nobody would escalate about will be cut, justified by the same usage numbers that looked healthy.

### Depth versus breadth

**Breadth** is what proportion of the eligible population uses the system; **depth** is how much of a user's relevant work passes through it. They are independent and demand different interventions.

| Pattern | Reading | Intervention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wide and shallow | Everybody tried it, nobody relies on it. Usually a novelty curve, sometimes a genuinely narrow capability oversold | Narrow the claim, deepen one workflow, stop the general campaign |
| Narrow and deep | A real capability serving a real population. The healthiest early state | Expand by adjacent workflow, not by adjacent department |
| Wide and deep | Working. Now the second-order effects of 10.3 become the operating agenda | Watch reviewer load and dependency, not usage |
| Narrow and shallow | Nothing is happening. Do not scale, do not relaunch | Return to the use-case selection question. The task may be wrong |

**Decision rule: pursue depth before breadth, because a deep narrow deployment produces evidence and a wide shallow one produces only a number.**

### Usage is not value

The gap between them is where most artificial intelligence business cases quietly fail. **Usage** is an activity count; **value** is a change in a business outcome the organization measured before the system existed. Four properties separate them.

1. Usage can rise while value falls: a system that makes drafting cheap increases drafts, which increases review, which increases cycle time. Usage doubled; the outcome got worse.
2. Usage is available on day one; value requires the baseline that had to exist before launch, the strongest argument for measuring the current process during discovery.
3. Usage is attributable to the system; value almost never is cleanly, so the attribution method and its limits are stated rather than hidden.
4. Usage is the metric a vendor will offer you: a reason for suspicion, not comfort.

The value metrics that survive scrutiny predate the system: cycle time on a named process, cost per completed matter, error or rework rate, escalation volume, throughput per full-time equivalent and the specific regulatory or client service level the function is measured on. Anything measured only since launch is a program metric, not a business one.

### Cohort retention for internal tools

Internal tools deserve the same cohort discipline as consumer products and almost never get it: group users by activation week, then plot the proportion of each cohort still active by week since activation.

```
  % of cohort active, by weeks since activation

  100 |*
      | *
   80 |  *                             healthy: falls, then FLATTENS
      |   *  *                         onto a plateau. The plateau
   60 |      \  *  *                   height is the real adoption
      |       \       *  *  *  *  *    number, not week-one usage
   40 |        \
      |         \
   20 |          \                     unhealthy: keeps falling.
      |           \                    no plateau means no habitual
    0 |            \____ ____ ____     population is forming
      +----+----+----+----+----+----
        2    4    6    8   10   12  weeks
```

Three readings are the whole diagnostic. **A curve that flattens** has found a real user population, and the plateau height times the eligible population is the honest forecast. **A curve that keeps falling** has no habitual population, and scaling it multiplies churn. **A later cohort with a lower plateau than an earlier one** means the product degraded, the onboarding degraded or the later population was different in kind; resolve it before further rollout, because the trend continues.

Novelty is the confound. Weeks one and two of every cohort overstate. Read the plateau, never the peak.

### The abandoned user

The most information-dense population in the deployment and the one nobody interviews. Define **abandonment** operationally: activated, then no real-work usage for four consecutive weeks. Run the exit interview, because the reason will not be in the telemetry.

The six reasons, in the order they usually turn out to be true:

1. It was wrong on the case they cared about, once, early, and they stopped trusting the whole class.
2. Reviewing the output took longer than doing the task: the saving was on the wrong step.
3. Their actual work is not the work the system was built for, and the mismatch showed on contact.
4. They could not get it to work and asking for help had a social cost.
5. Their manager measures something the system does not improve.
6. Something changed in the system, silently, and their working method stopped working.

Reason one is a trust event, covered below. Reason two is a workflow design defect, covered in 10.3 as workload displacement. Reason five is misread as user resistance when it is a correctly functioning incentive system pointed elsewhere; fix it by changing what the manager is measured on, not by persuading the user.

### Segment; never average

An aggregate adoption number averages populations with nothing in common, destroying the signal you need. Segment by **role** first, because role determines the task, then by tenure, business unit and jurisdiction where entitlement or regulation differs.

The characteristic finding, recurring across enterprises: senior practitioners show low usage and high value per use; junior practitioners show high usage and variable value; the middle tier the highest total value and the highest risk, because they use it heavily and review it least. The distribution is invisible in the average and determines where the review controls and the training spend belong.

## 7.4 Training and enablement

### Curriculum architecture by audience

**Seven audiences**, seven objectives, seven formats. A single course for everyone teaches the wrong thing to six of them.

| Audience | Objective | Format | Duration | The thing they must leave with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Executive** | Decide and sponsor competently; know what they are accountable for | Briefing plus a live failure demonstration | 60 to 90 minutes, once, refreshed semiannually | What the organization has accepted, what it has not and which three decisions are theirs |
| **Manager** | Redesign the work, set expectations, handle the accountability question from their team | Workshop on job design and measurement | Half day plus a follow-up at week six | How their team's work and metrics change, and what they now supervise |
| **Power user** | Operate at the edge of the capability and generate templates and corrections others reuse | Hands-on lab on real matters | 2 days plus an ongoing community | Advanced technique plus an obligation to feed corrections back |
| **General user** | Do their existing task through the system, safely | Just-in-time, in the workflow, plus a 45-minute grounding | 45 minutes plus embedded guidance | The task, the limits and the escalation path |
| **Reviewer** | Detect wrong output efficiently; know when to reject rather than repair | Calibration exercise on seeded errors | 1 day, then quarterly recalibration | A tested ability to catch the errors this system actually makes |
| **Builder** | Design, evaluate and change the system safely | Technical program plus supervised delivery | 5 days plus mentored build | Evaluation discipline before capability |
| **Control owner** | Operate and evidence the control they own, including its failure behavior | Control walkthrough plus evidence rehearsal | Half day, annually | What their control does when it fails, and where the artifact lives |

**Decision rule: build the reviewer curriculum before the user curriculum, because a population that can use the system faster than it can check the system is a population producing unreviewed output at scale.**

### The four things that must be taught and that nobody expects

Standard enablement teaches capability. Capability is the least important quarter of what a regulated enterprise must teach.

1. **What the system cannot do.** Stated concretely and by class, not as a disclaimer. "It does not know anything filed after the corpus cut. It cannot see the matter file unless it is in the document management system. It will not tell you when a controlling authority was superseded." A user who cannot name three specific limits has not been trained.
2. **How to recognize a wrong answer.** This is a teachable skill and it is system-specific. The characteristic error signature of a retrieval system is a fluent answer built on a plausible but non-controlling source. The characteristic error signature of a long-context summarization step is a confident omission. Teach the signature of this system's errors using seeded examples the trainee grades and then sees graded.
3. **When to escalate, expressed as a trigger rather than a judgment.** "Escalate if the output concerns an entity on the restricted list, if the matter value exceeds the threshold, if the system's citation cannot be opened, or if you disagree with the output and cannot say why." Judgment-based escalation rules produce escalation rates near zero.
4. **The accountability position.** Stated in one sentence, taught in every curriculum and repeated in the interface: **the user remains responsible for the output.** The system is an instrument. Using it does not transfer professional responsibility, does not satisfy a duty of competence and will not be accepted as an explanation by a regulator, a court, a client or an internal disciplinary process. ⚠ For regulated professionals the precise formulation is a matter for counsel and for the relevant professional body's guidance, and it should be reviewed rather than drafted by the program team.

### Licensing to use

**Licensing to use** means access is contingent on demonstrated competence rather than on employment. It is heavy-handed, it slows rollout and it is correct in exactly three situations: where the output enters a regulated record, where the user can cause an irreversible external effect, and where a professional body or a regulator expects demonstrated competence in the tools used to discharge a duty.

Where warranted, the license has four properties: a short assessment that includes error recognition rather than only capability, an expiry, a suspension mechanism triggered by a quality incident and a register that names who holds it. A license with no expiry and no suspension is a training record wearing a stronger word.

Where not warranted, do not impose it. An access barrier applied to a low-stakes assistant produces a workaround, and the workaround is the ungoverned consumer tool the program exists to displace.

### Just-in-time versus classroom

Classroom enablement transfers understanding of the frame: what this is, what it is not, who is accountable, what happens when it is wrong. That content is genuinely durable and belongs in a session with a human in the room.

Everything procedural belongs **in the workflow at the moment of use**: the prompt template surfaced in the interface, the limitation stated on the screen where the limit binds, the escalation button in the review pane, the worked example in the tooltip. Procedural training delivered in a classroom four weeks before first use has an effective retention approaching zero, and every enterprise that has measured this has found the same thing.

**Decision rule: teach the frame in a room and the procedure in the interface, and if a piece of training cannot be placed in the interface, ask whether the workflow is designed correctly.**

## 7.5 Building the capability: teams, workflows and enablement

A capability is built when the organization can run its systems without depending on the people who designed them. That is the measure of enablement, the team's independence rather than the architect's productivity, and it is the same standard the handoff discipline of 8.11 applies at system level. Four structures produce that independence: a deliberate capability ladder, a sourcing rule for each rung, team working practices that distribute through version control rather than through memory, and the enablement mechanisms of champions and communities.

### The capability ladder

Four rungs, and the population at each rung should be an explicit target with an explicit ratio, because the ratios determine what the organization can do without external help.

| Rung | Can do | Must know | Healthy band for this rung alone, in a 1,000-person enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Consumer** | Use a deployed system for their own task, safely, and recognize when it is wrong | Limits, escalation, accountability position | 600 to 900 |
| **Configurer** | Build prompts, templates and small automations within a governed platform; curate a corpus | Evaluation basics, data classification, where the guardrails are and why | 50 to 150 |
| **Builder** | Design and ship a system: retrieval, tools, evaluation harness, observability | The seven primitives, evaluation design, failure modes, cost model | 10 to 30 |
| **Architect** | Decide whether to build at all, own the operating model, sign the design | Everything a builder knows plus governance, economics, the regulatory surface and the exit | 2 to 5 |

**The bands are read one at a time rather than summed.** Each states a healthy range for its own rung against a 1,000-person population, and the four maxima deliberately exceed 1,000 because no organization should sit at the top of all four. An organization at the top of every band has over-invested in the upper rungs, which shows up as builders and architects with no delivered systems to own and a configurer population large enough that the review capacity behind it does not exist.

The steep and commonly missed transition is consumer to configurer, because it is the first rung where a person can create something other people rely on. **A configurer population without evaluation discipline is the mechanism by which shadow artificial intelligence enters a governed enterprise.** Govern that rung explicitly: a platform they build inside, a review before anything is shared beyond the team and a register of what exists.

The builder-to-architect transition is different in kind rather than degree. A builder is accountable for whether the system works. An architect is accountable for whether it should exist, who runs it, what it does to the people around it and how it ends. That distinction is the subject of Part 10.

### Hire, build or contract

| Capability | Default source | Reasoning | The mistake |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Architect | Hire or promote internally | Requires deep organizational and regulatory context that a contractor cannot acquire in the engagement window | Contracting the architecture and owning only the build. The organization then cannot change the system it depends on |
| Builder | Build internally, seed with contract | Genuinely teachable to strong engineers in months; retention of design knowledge matters more than speed | Hiring scarce specialist titles at a premium for work an internal engineer will do better with domain knowledge |
| Configurer | Build internally, always | It is the domain expert learning a tool. Outsourcing it outsources the domain knowledge that is the actual asset | Treating configuration as a technical function and staffing it from engineering |
| Specialist evaluation, red teaming, assurance | Contract, deliberately | Independence has value here. The internal team should not grade its own homework | Building internal red teaming and then reporting it to the delivery lead |
| Second-line technical challenge | Hire, small and senior | Per the competence inversion in Part 4, an oversight function that cannot read a design has no challenge capability | Buying a questionnaire tool and calling it oversight |

**Decision rule: contract what benefits from independence or scarcity, hire what requires organizational context and never contract the accountability.**

### Team setup: shared versus personal

One organizing principle answers most questions about team-level configuration: **shared versus personal**. Anything the whole team needs goes in the project, in version control, so everyone who checks it out receives it: conventions, shared capability configuration, standard procedures. Anything personal stays in the individual's environment where it affects nobody else.

| Goes in the project, version-controlled | Stays personal |
| --- | --- |
| Team conventions and standards | Individual preferences |
| Shared capability configuration | Experimental setups |
| Standard procedures the team runs | Personal shortcuts |
| Path-scoped rules for file types | Anything you would not want to impose |

**The diagnostic pattern:** a new team member is not receiving the team's conventions. The cause: someone put them in a personal location, where version control cannot distribute them. The fix: move them to the project.

Four supporting practices:

- **Credentials by reference, never by value.** Environment-variable expansion so configuration can be committed without committing secrets.
- **Split large configurations** into focused topic files rather than one growing monolith.
- **Scope rules to the files they govern**, so conventions follow file type wherever it lives rather than depending on directory location. The canonical case is a convention that applies to test files, which are scattered through every directory: a directory-bound file cannot chase them, and a single root file relies on the model inferring which section applies.
- **Generate the initial conventions file from the codebase** rather than writing it from nothing.

**The selection rule.** If it should apply to everything, it is a convention; if it is a procedure invoked when needed, it is a capability. The same progressive-disclosure logic as 2.3 and 2.6.

#### The spend posture belongs in team setup, not in operations

8.10 sets out the budget guardrails a running system needs. **A subset of them are administrative settings that belong in the team configuration, decided before anyone logs in rather than discovered on an invoice**, and inheriting the defaults is a decision taken by omission.

| Setting | What it decides |
| --- | --- |
| **Model default** | Which tier a session starts on, which is the tier most work will run on because most users never change it |
| **Model allowlist or restriction** | Which tiers the team may switch to at all |
| **Effort guidance** | How hard the model works on a task by default |
| **Spend, rate and per-user caps** | The bound on consumption, per person rather than only in aggregate |

**The reason these belong at setup rather than at review is multiplication.** 2.6 establishes that an absent tier decision defaults to the most expensive option. At individual scale that is a line item. **Across dozens of people and every request they make, the same omission is the whole cost curve**, and by the time it is visible in a monthly review the team has built habits around it. The per-user cap is the one most often skipped and the one that localizes a problem: an aggregate cap tells you the organization overspent, and a per-user cap tells you where.

### The four development workflows

| Workflow | Use when | The mistake to reject |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plan first** | Large changes, multi-file work, architectural decisions, anything with several credible approaches. Explore, understand dependencies and propose an approach before changing anything | "Start directly and switch to planning if complexity emerges" is wrong **when the complexity is already stated in the requirements** |
| **Direct execution** | Small well-scoped changes with a clear cause | Planning a one-line fix is over-process |
| **Test first** | Behavior can be specified in advance, including edge cases. An objective finish line removes the argument about whether it is done | Writing code then tests inverts the finish line |
| **Independent review** | Always, for anything consequential | Self-review, because whatever produced the work retains the reasoning that produced the errors |

**Two mechanics** support all four: reusable procedures stored in the project rather than retyped, with a placeholder for the part that varies per invocation; and isolated working copies when several instances work in parallel, so they do not overwrite each other.

**Automated pipelines** add four rules: run non-interactively, or the pipeline waits forever for input that never comes; request machine-readable output so findings can be consumed programmatically; supply project conventions so generated work matches house standards; and **when re-running a review after new changes, supply the previous findings and ask only for what is new or still outstanding**, or the same comments get posted repeatedly and developers stop reading them. Developer trust is a finite resource and duplicate or wrong findings spend it; a review system that is technically accurate and universally ignored has failed.

### AI-assisted delivery: four integration points and their measurement

The four development workflows describe how one engineer works. The four integration points describe where the capability attaches to the delivery pipeline, which is the level at which an architect is asked to approve it. Each one has a characteristic failure and a measurement that tells you whether it is working.

| Integration point | What it does | Characteristic failure | What to measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Change review** | Runs on every proposed change, posts findings against the diff | Volume. A reviewer that comments on everything trains the team to dismiss everything, and the dismissal generalizes to the findings that mattered | Finding acceptance rate, segmented by finding category. A category below roughly one in five accepted should be switched off, not tuned |
| **Test generation** | Proposes tests for new or changed behavior | Tests written against the implementation rather than the specification, which pass permanently and detect nothing. Generated tests inherit the defect they were meant to catch | Mutation survival, or at minimum whether a deliberately introduced defect is caught. A generated suite that has never failed has not been shown to work |
| **Pipeline gating** | Blocks a merge on a condition the agent evaluates | Non-determinism at a gate. The same change passing on one run and failing on the next destroys the gate's authority faster than a wrong result does | Gate flip rate on unchanged input. Anything above a low single-digit percentage means the gate is advisory whatever the policy says |
| **Documentation generation** | Produces or updates documentation from the code and the change history | Fluent documentation that describes intent rather than behavior, which is worse than absent documentation because it is trusted | Whether a reader can complete the described task without asking the author. Sampled, not asserted |

**The review asymmetry is the governing economics of all four.** Generation is cheap and review is not, so every integration point increases the volume of work presented for human judgment while leaving the human judgment capacity unchanged. A pipeline that produces more proposals than the team can genuinely review has not accelerated delivery, it has moved the queue and hidden it. Size each integration point against review capacity, not against generation capacity, and treat an unreviewed merge as the defect it is rather than as throughput.

⧉ **The unmeasured rollout is the dominant failure.** Teams deploy all four integration points, report adoption in seats and never establish whether delivery improved. The instrument already exists and is the one the engineering function already reports: lead time for change, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore service. Take a baseline before the rollout, not after, because a baseline taken after deployment measures the system you already changed. Change failure rate is the one that decides the argument: a program that raises deployment frequency and raises change failure rate in the same quarter has moved work downstream into incidents, and the productivity claim is unearned.

**Generated code carries three exposures that a human-written commit does not raise in the same way**, and each belongs to an existing control rather than to a new one. License provenance, because a generated fragment may reproduce licensed material and the obligation attaches at distribution (4.14). Dependency introduction, because an agent will add a package to solve a problem and the package arrives without the diligence a human addition would attract. And pattern propagation, because a plausible but flawed approach spreads at repository scale, which makes remediation a fleet-wide change whose effort grows with adoption rather than a single fix.

### The verification checklist, and the dimension nobody writes down

The review asymmetry above says that generation is cheap and review is not. **The checklist is what stops that asymmetry from being resolved in favor of whatever is fastest**, and it is a deliverable the team writes for itself rather than a policy handed to it. Four dimensions, and the fourth is the one that is almost never stated.

| Dimension | The check, stated concretely |
| --- | --- |
| **Correctness** | Tests exist and pass, and the behavior matches the stated requirement including the edge cases the requirement implies |
| **Security** | No secrets in the code, inputs are validated, and any tool or external call uses least-privilege access |
| **Maintainability** | It reads clearly, follows the team's conventions, and carries no unexplained complexity |
| **Human understanding** | **The person submitting the change can explain what it does and why, including how it handles inputs it was not explicitly tested against** |

⧉ **The fourth dimension is the one that catches what the first three cannot, because the first three are all satisfiable by output nobody understands.** A generated change passes review and passes tests, reaches production and leaks data through an input it never validated. In the post-incident review the author cannot say why the code handled that input as it did. It looked plausible, the tests were green, and nothing in the process asked the only question that would have stopped it.

**Name the failure mode: judgment erosion.** It is distinct from the volume problem in the review asymmetry and it moves in the opposite direction. Volume degrades review by giving reviewers too much to read. Judgment erosion degrades it by giving them something that reads well, passes its checks, and is understood by nobody, so **the review is performed accurately on the wrong basis.** Speed has replaced understanding, and the team gets faster and less able to explain what it ships in the same motion.

**Automate every check that can be automated, and note which one cannot.** A regression suite and an eval set convert correctness and behavior from a reviewer's judgment call into a gate that runs on every change, which is the point of 8.2 and 8.3 applied to the team's own output rather than to the system's. **The human-understanding check is the one that cannot be automated**, because its subject is the reviewer rather than the artifact, and that is precisely why it has to be written down. A checklist that omits it has automated the three checks that were never the binding constraint.

### The champion network and its failure mode

A **champion network** is a distributed set of local, credible practitioners who provide first-line help, gather feedback and carry legitimacy the program office does not have. It works, and it has one dominant failure mode that repeats in every enterprise: **the role is unfunded.** Champions are volunteers with existing full workloads, chosen because they were enthusiastic, given a title and no time. Within one quarter the network is nominally intact and functionally dead, and the program keeps reporting champion coverage as an adoption asset.

The five conditions that make a champion network real: allocated time expressed as a percentage and visible to their line manager, a named owner they report into for this purpose, a feedback channel that demonstrably changes the system, recognition that appears in their performance record and a term with a renewal. Miss the first and the rest are decoration.

### Communities of practice and the internal credential

A **community of practice** is the mechanism by which technique propagates without going through the program office. It requires a cadence, a curated agenda, real artifacts shared rather than slides and at least one person whose job includes running it. Communities that meet without artifacts become social; communities without an owner stop meeting inside two quarters.

The **internal credential** is worth building at the configurer rung and above once the population passes roughly one hundred, and it does three things: it makes capability legible for staffing decisions, it creates a career reason to invest personal time, and it gives the governance function a defensible answer to the competence question a regulator or a client will eventually ask. Keep it small, assess by producing something rather than by multiple choice, and expire it.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise questions this section does not ask.** Which capabilities sit with a central platform team, which sit inside the business function and which are bought, because running without the architect is an operating model question rather than a knowledge transfer question. Who is provisioned, on what tier, deprovisioned when they leave, and which cost center receives the invoice, because shared versus personal configuration is the second question a rollout raises. And does an AI review satisfy the control requiring a production change to be reviewed by someone other than its author, and who owns a defect it passed?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Running it without depending on you | Deciding where each capability sits across platform, function and vendor | Target operating model, owned by the chief information officer or equivalent |
| Treating enablement as training | Naming the number of people whose simultaneous absence stops the system, and setting a target | Key person risk entry, owned by the service owner |
| Success as the architect's absence | Measuring how often the original designer is paged into incidents | Escalation metric, owned by operations |
| Distributing conventions through version control | Group-based entitlement through the corporate directory, with joiner, mover and leaver handling | Entitlement register, owned by identity management |
| Rolling the tooling to a team | Cost attribution per team or business unit with a budget and an alert threshold | Chargeback or showback model, owned by finance |
| Keeping credentials by reference | Enterprise retention setting and the policy on what may be entered | Data handling policy, owned by the data protection officer |
| Standardizing on sanctioned tooling | Detecting unsanctioned tool use on company data | Detection rule, owned by security |
| Independent review as a workflow | Whether an AI review satisfies separation of duties, and who is accountable for what it misses | Change control policy, owned by the change advisory board |
| Direct execution on small changes | Traceability from every production change to an approved ticket | Change record, owned by the release manager |
| Generated code entering the repository | Static analysis, dependency scanning, secret scanning and license provenance | Secure development standard, owned by application security |
| Improving developer workflows | Baseline and target for lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate and restore time | Metrics baseline, owned by the engineering lead |

**What this costs the organization.** Key person dependency is priced only when the person resigns, and by then the replacement cost includes rediscovering decisions never written down; an architect who remains the escalation path for the last system delivers the current one more slowly, on a different budget. Without an acceptance step in which a receiving operations owner signs that the run team is capable, the build team is released on a date rather than on readiness, the shortfall appears as incident volume in the first quarter of run, and the original team answers questions informally for months as shadow support, booked to no cost center. Unattributed consumption arrives as an invoice nobody owns, and the response is usually a spending freeze that stalls the adoption it was meant to create; leavers holding seats for months are both a license charge and an access finding. Generated code spreads a plausible but flawed pattern at repository scale, so remediation is a fleet-wide change whose effort scales with adoption, and licensing exposure in generated code and pulled dependencies surfaces during due diligence, long after the commit.

**The executive translation.** Dependence on one designer sits on the risk register with a target number, not in the staffing plan as a preference. The tooling rollout is a licensing, identity and cost attribution program with a configuration convention inside it, not a configuration exercise with an invoice attached. AI-assisted development passes the same change control as everything else, and change failure rate is shown before and after. Handover completes when the operations owner signs that they can run it, not when the build team finishes building it.

## 7.6 Trust

### Trust is engineered, not communicated

Trust in an enterprise artificial intelligence system is a **behavioral property of the deployed system**, produced by what it does in front of users. Messaging cannot raise it, and messaging while the behavior is unchanged lowers it, because the message becomes evidence that the program is managing perception rather than accuracy.

**Seven things build it**, each a design decision with a cost:

1. **Accuracy on the cases the user cares about**, rarely the cases the aggregate metric covers. Segment the evaluation set by what users find important, not by what is easy to label.
2. **Citations that resolve**: the user can open the source and see the sentence. An unopenable citation is worse than none, because it invites verification then defeats it.
3. **Admitting uncertainty**, calibrated. A system that says it does not know, and is right to say so, buys more trust per instance than several correct answers.
4. **Consistent behavior**: the same input produces recognizably the same class of output tomorrow. Users build working methods on observed behavior, and silent variance destroys them.
5. **Visible human control**: the user can see where a person can stop, override or correct the system and knows how to invoke it.
6. **Fast, visible correction of errors.** The interval between a user reporting a wrong answer and seeing evidence of a fix is among the highest-leverage numbers in the program.
7. **Honest limits, published.** The known-limitations document is a trust instrument, not a legal shield. Users told what it cannot do forgive it for not doing that.

**Four things destroy it**, and the asymmetry in magnitude is the point:

1. **One confident wrong answer in a high-stakes case.** Not many. One, if it lands in front of the right person on the wrong matter. The cost is the whole class of use, not the instance.
2. **Silent behavior change.** A model upgrade or prompt change that alters output style or judgment without notice breaks every working method built on the previous behavior, and the user reads it as unreliability rather than change.
3. **Opacity.** No sources, no reasoning, no way to tell why. Professionals do not adopt instruments they cannot interrogate; that is professional instinct, not resistance.
4. **A control that is obviously theater.** A review step nobody has time to perform, a confirmation dialog everyone clicks through, an approval that is always granted. Visible theater teaches the population that the whole control set is decorative, and generalizes instantly to controls that are real.

### The trust asymmetry and the first ninety days

⧉ **Trust is lost at roughly ten times the rate it is earned, and the first ninety days set a ceiling the program will not exceed later.** It is the biggest risk in organizational adoption and almost never budgeted for, because the cost falls in a later period than the decision that caused it.

Three consequences follow, each a design instruction:

**Launch narrow.** Ship where the system is strongest, even if the value is smaller: the first ninety days purchase a reputation, not a return. A launch across the full task surface guarantees early failures in the weakest segment, attributed to the system as a whole.

**Over-invest in the first cohort.** Named support, response within hours, personal follow-up on every reported error. Expensive per user, cheap per program, because that cohort becomes the reference the rest of the organization asks.

**Never let a high-stakes error go uncorrected in public view.** Correct it, tell the user what changed, and add the case to the evaluation set so the fix is durable and demonstrable. The recovery is the trust-building event; the error alone is not fatal, and unacknowledged errors are.

The corollary for the executive conversation in Part 9: a program that launches broadly to show ambition optimizes the wrong variable, and the cost lands two quarters later disguised as user resistance.

## 7.7 Change management

### Applying a change framework without reciting one

Stripped to what binds in an enterprise artificial intelligence deployment, the standard sequence is four obligations. Establish **why now**: a pressure the affected population already feels rather than a technology that has arrived. Build a **guiding coalition that includes the skeptical function**, because a coalition of enthusiasts cannot deliver the organization. Produce **visible early results in the affected population's own terms**: their cycle time and their workload, not the program's usage chart. Then **anchor the change in the operating system of the organization**: role descriptions, performance measures, procedures, quality standards and the audit plan. Nearly every program stops before the fourth, and reverts within two cycles because nothing structural changed.

**Decision rule: a change is anchored when the old way is no longer described in the process documentation and no longer measurable in the performance system, and until then it is a pilot with wide distribution.**

### Stakeholder mapping and resistance analysis

Map every affected group on two axes, influence over the outcome and current disposition, then treat each quadrant differently.

```
                 HIGH INFLUENCE
                       |
   BLOCKER             |            SPONSOR
   engage first,       |            use for air cover,
   privately, with     |            protect from
   their objection     |            over-promising
   in their language   |
                       |
  ---------------------+----------------------> SUPPORTIVE
   OPPONENT            |            ADVOCATE
   do not convert;     |            resource them,
   contain the         |            give them the
   objection with      |            first cohort,
   evidence and        |            harvest artifacts
   move                |
                       |
                 LOW INFLUENCE
```

The quadrant that consumes the most program time and returns the least is the low-influence opponent; the one that decides the program is the high-influence blocker: a blocker whose objection is heard becomes a condition-setter, and one whose objection is bypassed becomes an escalation.

Engagement carried as personal relationships does not survive a change of sponsor, and mid-build turnover is common enough to plan for: give every engagement that decides something a forum with a membership, a cadence and minutes, under terms of reference the sponsor owns. Without a record of what was decided and on what criterion, a new sponsor costs weeks of senior time rebuilding consensus and reopening settled trade-offs.

### The two legitimate resistances

Most resistance framing treats objection as irrational and reaches for persuasion. Two resistances are not irrational, and they matter most in professional and regulated environments; persuasion applied to either produces contempt.

**Professional identity.** For a lawyer, an underwriter, a clinician, a credit analyst or an engineer, judgment in the affected task is not a job function; it is the content of professional standing accumulated over a career. A system presented as performing that judgment is heard as a claim that the standing was not worth much. The response is not reassurance but redesign: the system does assembly, retrieval, first-pass extraction and consistency checking, the judgment call stays explicitly and visibly with the professional, and their throughput or reach increases. Where the honest answer is that the system does displace the judgment, say so and manage it as displacement rather than dressing it as augmentation, because the population will discover which it is within a month.

**Accountability exposure.** The reviewer is asked to sign for output they did not produce, cannot fully inspect and did not choose the method for: a real and correctly identified increase in personal exposure, and the objection most often dismissed as obstruction. It has four legitimate answers, all structural: the evidence to review efficiently, meaning sources, differences and confidence; time in the capacity model rather than an assumption that review is free; explicit authority to reject and to escalate without career cost; and a written statement, at the level of the organization rather than the individual, of who is accountable for a system-caused failure the reviewer could not reasonably have detected. ⚠ That written position is a matter for legal, for the insurer and in professional contexts for the relevant regulator's guidance, and it should be settled before rollout rather than after the first incident.

### Job design and role redefinition

Six artifacts must be revised, and that revision is the change management deliverable: the role description, the performance measures, the capacity model, the quality standard for the output, the supervision model for junior staff whose learning path the system alters and the career progression the function offers.

The capacity model is omitted most often and does the most damage. If a reviewer's establishment assumes eight matters a day of self-produced work and the new model routes twenty machine-produced drafts to that person, the establishment is wrong by a factor, and the quality collapse that follows will be reported as a model quality problem. It is not; it is a staffing model that was never updated.

1.3 raises all six from the other end and carries none of them, as the things a delegation map does not show: **moving work off people changes job descriptions, training, performance measures and, in some jurisdictions, consultation obligations.** The first three are the artifacts above. The fourth is the subject of the next subsection, and it is the one that can stop a rollout rather than merely embarrass it.

### ⚠ Union, works council and professional-body considerations

Where employees are represented, deployment of a system that monitors, measures, ranks or materially alters work is frequently subject to consultation or co-determination obligations before implementation, not after. In several European jurisdictions works council agreement is a precondition, not a courtesy, and the obligation can attach to the productivity telemetry as much as to the system itself. In professional contexts a supervisory body, a bar, a medical council or a financial regulator may have expectations about competence, supervision, delegation and disclosure to the client. These are not program-office judgments. ⚠ Obtain a jurisdiction-specific determination from counsel before any deployment that measures individual performance, alters a represented role or produces work product a professional signs, and treat it as a gate on the rollout rather than a workstream beside it.

### Communication cadence and message discipline

Four channels on three clocks. **Executive**, monthly, one page, the same six numbers each time so trend is readable. **Manager**, fortnightly, what changes for their team next and what they must do. **User**, at the moment of change plus a monthly digest of fixes, because the fixed list is the most-read communication the program produces. **Governance and control owners**, on the committee cycle, exceptions out of cycle.

Message discipline has five rules, each existing because its breach has cost a real program:

1. Never claim a capability the current build does not have, including next quarter's.
2. Never publish a number you cannot decompose if asked in the meeting.
3. Report failures before they are asked about, in the same channel and format as successes.
4. Use one vocabulary across all four channels. Divergent naming for the same thing is read as spin the moment two audiences compare notes.
5. Never let the communication get ahead of the enablement. Awareness created before access exists converts to cynicism, and the second campaign performs worse than the first.

### The people whose work the system absorbs

Stated honestly, because the euphemism is detected immediately and costs more than the truth.

If a system absorbs a category of work, either the volume of that work rises to fill the capacity, or the people who did it do different work, or there are fewer of them. Those are the only three outcomes. Which one applies is an executive decision, not a program decision, taken **before** rollout, because the population will ask in week one and the absence of an answer is itself an answer they will act on.

Four rules for handling it:

1. **Decide and state the position early.** Ambiguity is more destabilizing than an unwelcome but definite answer, and it corrupts the feedback the program receives: people who suspect the system threatens their role will not report its errors honestly. They will report them very honestly, or not at all, and you will not know which.
2. **Do not use "augmentation" as a synonym for "we have not decided."** If the honest answer is that headcount in a function will decline over three years through attrition, say that, with the timeframe and the mechanism.
3. **If redeployment is the answer, fund it as a program with named destination roles, training and a date.** Redeployment stated as a value and not funded as a plan is understood correctly by everyone as a phrase.
4. **Do not ask the displaced population to train the system without acknowledging what is being asked.** They will do it if treated as professionals with a stake in the outcome and the terms are explicit. Asked without acknowledgment, they will comply and the training data will be quietly poor, a failure undetectable in the telemetry.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** Which of these determinations has to be made before the pilot rather than before the rollout, given that a bounded pilot inside a represented workforce is already a deployment for this purpose and is the point at which the measurement starts.

**Governance at this decision.** Four rows, and the block deliberately stops there. **The capacity model is 2.12's**, whose block already carries arrival rate, review time, queue depth and headcount as a capacity and staffing plan owned by operations, and the third job-design artifact above is that plan under another name. **Training, communication and the measurement of adoption are 7.2's** adoption plan, and **access made contingent on demonstrated competence is 7.5's** entitlement register. Restating any of them here would put two owners on one artifact.

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deploying a system that monitors, measures, ranks or materially alters represented work | Whether consultation or co-determination is owed in each jurisdiction, and whether it gates the rollout date rather than running beside it ⚠ | Employee-representation determination per jurisdiction, dated and re-taken on material change. Employment counsel with the change lead |
| Instrumenting the workflow so adoption can be measured | Whether the productivity telemetry attracts the obligation on its own, separately from the system it measures, and which fields it covers | Monitoring position naming the measured fields and the population. Data protection officer with employment counsel |
| Redefining the role rather than only the task | Revising the role description, the performance measures, the quality standard, the supervision model and the career progression on one date rather than as they are noticed | Revised role and measurement set, owned by the function head with human resources |
| Producing work product a professional signs | What the supervisory body expects on competence, supervision, delegation and disclosure to the client ⚠ | Professional-body position, owned by whoever already answers to that body |

**What this costs the organization.** A consultation obligation discovered after the build is a delay priced in weeks of an idle delivery team, and where agreement is a precondition it is a rollout that cannot proceed on any budget. The cost people forget is the second determination: the productivity telemetry usually attracts the obligation in its own right, and it is specified by the measurement workstream months after the legal question was asked about the system.

**The executive translation.** In some of the jurisdictions we operate in this is a gate and not a consultation, the determination takes weeks to obtain, and it is cheaper to start it now than to hold a finished system at the border.

## 7.8 A worked adoption plan

A contract review assistant in an in-house legal function: 140 lawyers, 30 paralegals, four jurisdictions. First-pass review of inbound commercial contracts against a playbook: an issues list, suggested positions, a redline draft; the lawyer reviews, decides and signs. Discovery baseline: 47 minutes median first-pass review, 22 percent of issues missed against a labeled retrospective set, 11-day median cycle time, receipt to first business response.

| Phase | Duration | Population | What is built | Adoption gate to proceed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **0. Baseline and design** | 6 weeks | None | Labeled evaluation set of 300 historical contracts, baseline measurement, entitlement design across the four jurisdictions, accountability position drafted with counsel, reviewer curriculum designed first | Baseline measured and signed by the function head. Written accountability position issued. Works council position determined for the two jurisdictions requiring it ⚠ |
| **1. Proof of concept** | 4 weeks | Build team, 3 lawyers as graders | Retrieval over playbook and precedent, issue extraction, draft redline. No production data path | Recall on the labeled set at or above the human first-pass rate on the three highest-volume contract types. Otherwise stop and report |
| **2. Pilot** | 10 weeks | 24 lawyers, representative draw across all four jurisdictions and all seniority bands, not volunteers. Matched holdout of 24 running current process | Production data path, production entitlement model, full instrumentation, in-workflow entry point inside the contract lifecycle system, escalation button, correction capture writing to the evaluation set | Pre-registered: median first-pass under 25 minutes, issue miss rate at or below 22 percent, no unreviewed output reaching a counterparty, week-8 cohort retention plateau above 60 percent. Kill criterion: any counterparty-facing error attributable to unreviewed output, or miss rate above baseline at week 4 |
| **3. Scale wave one** | 8 weeks | Two largest jurisdictions, all 82 lawyers | Champion network funded at 10 percent time, reviewer calibration for the 30 paralegals, capacity model revised, role descriptions and performance measures updated | Activation above 80 percent, habitual above 55 percent at week 6, quality inside band by segment, no segment below baseline |
| **4. Scale wave two** | 8 weeks | Remaining two jurisdictions plus paralegal population | Jurisdiction-specific playbooks, second-line technical review completed, internal credential issued to configurers | Same gates, plus segment parity across jurisdictions or an explicit accepted exception |
| **5. Anchor** | 12 weeks | Whole function | Old process removed from documentation, audit plan updated, quality standard rewritten, supervision model for junior lawyers revised, dependency and reviewer-load monitoring live | Dependency above 40 percent, plateau stable across three consecutive cohorts, reviewer load inside the revised capacity model |

Metrics at every gate, definitions fixed: six funnel stages by role, jurisdiction and seniority; cohort retention plateau; median and 90th-percentile first-pass minutes; issue miss rate against the labeled set by contract type; escalation rate; correction rate; fully loaded cost per reviewed contract including lawyer minutes; and cycle time to first business response, the only one the business cares about.

The two likeliest gates to fail, named now so failing is a finding, not a surprise: the phase 2 week-8 plateau, because review burden may exceed drafting saving for senior lawyers, and phase 4 segment parity, because the smallest jurisdiction's playbook corpus is thinnest and retrieval follows it.

## Organizational Adoption: the one-page version

1. Adoption fails in three ways: nobody uses it, people use it and stop, people use it wrongly. Each has a different diagnosis and a fix that worsens the other two if misapplied, so diagnose before intervening.
2. A proof of concept, a pilot, a production rollout and a science project are four different things with different entry and exit criteria. **Any activity whose result changes no stated decision is a science project.**
3. Pilots need eight elements including a pre-registered threshold and a kill criterion, or they produce impressions. Pilot purgatory has four structural causes, and conditional scale funding removes the worst of them. **The worked plan runs the same discipline across six phases**, each carrying an adoption gate to proceed and each building on the production data path rather than on scaffolding, and it names the two gates most likely to fail in advance so that failing one is a finding rather than a surprise.
4. The successful pilot that cannot scale fails on population, scaffolding, volume economics or an entitlement model that twelve users hid.
5. Measure the six-stage funnel by ratio and by role, read cohort curves at the plateau, and interview the abandoned. **Never confuse usage with value, because usage rises when the system worsens.**
6. Build seven curricula, reviewer first, and teach the four things nobody expects: what it cannot do, how a wrong answer looks, when to escalate stated as a trigger, and that the user remains responsible for the output.
7. Build the capability ladder deliberately and govern the configurer rung, because that is where shadow artificial intelligence enters.
8. Team configuration is shared against personal, shared meaning in the project under version control. Set the spend posture at setup rather than at review.
9. Development work selects among plan first, direct execution, test first and independent review, and automated pipelines run non-interactively with previous findings supplied on re-runs.
10. Hold generated work to a verification checklist whose fourth dimension is human understanding, because the first three are all satisfiable by output nobody can explain.
11. Trust is an engineered property with seven builders and four destroyers. It is lost ten times faster than earned and the first ninety days set the ceiling, so launch narrow.
12. Anchor the change in role descriptions, performance measures and the capacity model, or it reverts.
13. The two legitimate resistances are professional identity and accountability exposure, and both need structural answers.
14. ⚠ Works council, union and professional-body obligations are gates determined by counsel.
15. Say honestly what happens to the people whose work is absorbed, before rollout, because ambiguity poisons the feedback the program runs on.
